VCF Museum · Exhibit Concept ReviewRev 3

Take both doors off and let the machine hold the screen

Two revisions built a wooden box with three real buttons and hung it on the door hinges. This one throws the box away. Both doors come off and go into storage, a length of steel conduit stands on the cabinet floor, and a 23.8″ touchscreen hangs off it on a monitor arm — with the card cage open behind it. Nothing is cut, drilled, or fastened to the machine.

The interface

The three buttons moved into the glass

Same three commands the docents reviewed — Back, Home, Next — and the same screens. They are touch targets now instead of 30 mm switches, pinned to the bottom of the display where a hand naturally lands. No swiping, no gestures, nothing hidden. Try it.

Tap Back · Home · Next — or use the ← → keys

23.8″IPS touchscreen, portrait
1080 × 1920Native portrait pixels
2″Touch target height
38″Touch row AFF — unchanged

Why targets and not swipe. A visitor gives a kiosk about three seconds to show what it does. Nothing on a screen says swipe; a button says press me. Gesture-only navigation also fails WCAG 2.5.1, which requires every function to work with a single pointer and no path-based gesture — and this audience skews older than the phone-native default.

Keeping the same three commands means the reviewed content, the screen order and the docent-approved wording all survive the pivot untouched. If we ever go back to physical buttons, the same app runs.

The cabinet · drawn to scale

With the doors on, and with them off

The machine is 71″ tall and 24″ wide, standing on 3⅛″ feet. The outer louvered door hangs on two pins, top and bottom — it lifts off. So does the perforated steel inner panel behind it. Both get bagged and stored, and both go back at the end of the exhibit's life.

  • Cabinet, measured
  • Added hardware — conduit, arm, screen
  • Dimension
  • ADA datum, 38″ above the floor

The dashed red line is the whole argument. In Rev 1 and Rev 2 it was where three anti-vandal switches were going to sit. In Rev 3 it is where the on-screen touch row sits. The mechanism changed completely and the datum did not move an inch — because it was never ours to move. ADA §308 sets it, and everything else in the design is placed from it.

Rev 2 → Rev 3

What this revision throws away

Rev 2 was a complete, checked, buildable design: a solid-pine box, nine crosscuts, a CNC-routed aluminium-composite face plate, twenty-one threaded inserts. It would have worked. It also cost a couple of hundred dollars, a week of careful work, and carried a real risk of looking homemade.

 Rev 1 & 2Rev 3
Display24″ panel behind a cut face plate23.8″ IPS touchscreen, bought off the shelf
InputThree 30 mm anti-vandal switchesThree on-screen touch targets
EnclosureSolid pine box, MDF back, ACM faceNone — the cabinet is the enclosure
MountBox hung on the outer door's hinge pinsConduit spine on the cabinet floor
DoorsOuter door removed, inner door keptBoth removed and stored
Fabrication9 crosscuts · 21 inserts · a routed panelCut one length of conduit
Load on the machine~150 lb in a clamp jaw, or bending on the pins~7.5 lb at each of two padded contacts
Touch row height38″ AFF38″ AFF — unchanged

Why the conduit, and not the arm's own desk clamp. A 20 lb screen reaching 15″ out makes a 300 in-lb overturning moment. A desk clamp has to swallow that across a two-inch jaw — about 150 lb of bite, and there is nothing on this machine we are willing to bite. Capture the same conduit at two points 40″ apart and the identical moment becomes a couple of about 7.5 lb at each end — a load you can take on a felt-faced foot and a padded top bracket. Twenty times gentler, and the hinge pins never see any of it.

The spine goes on the left — the same side the doors hinge from. That jamb has carried a door for forty years, so it is the more likely of the two to offer a rigid anchor for the straps. Which side the power supply modules sit on is still unconfirmed; the drawing puts them opposite the spine.

Before anyone buys anything

Five things still unanswered

  • Gate 1
    Does the monitor come back after a power cut?

    The museum kills power at night. If the screen wakes into standby and needs a button pressed, the exhibit is dark until a docent notices — which is exactly the failure this project exists to avoid. Test it with a power strip before the return window closes.

  • Gate 2
    Does Linux see the touch, and does it rotate with the screen?

    Most of these panels are standard USB HID digitizers and the Raspberry Pi picks them up without drivers. But rotating the display to portrait does not rotate the touch coordinates — that needs a transformation matrix set by hand. Two separate things to prove.

  • Gate 3
    Does the conduit fit the arm's collar?

    Monitor arm poles run about Ø38 mm; 1¼″ EMT is 1.510″. Close enough to be a problem — a few thousandths oversize and the collar will not go on at all. Caliper the supplied pole first, and err small so a shim can make up the difference.

  • Gate 4
    How tall is the door opening?

    Still the one dimension nobody has confirmed. There is a ~48″ tape reading from the site visit but no note of what it spanned. The conduit is cut to this number, so it is measured before anything is cut.

  • Gate 5
    Is the museum willing to expose the boards?

    The perforated inner door is what currently protects the card cage from forty thousand fingers a year. Removing it is what makes the exhibit worth looking at, and it is a curatorial call — the alternative is polycarbonate in the aperture.

One trade to accept knowingly. Three physical buttons at 38″ with a light press were genuinely accessible — tactile, findable without sight, compliant by construction. A touchscreen is not, and no amount of large type fixes that completely. Big high-contrast targets and an audio track mitigate it. This is a real cost of the pivot and the docents should agree to it deliberately rather than discover it after installation.

Concept, not a built exhibit. The screens are the docent-reviewed draft content. The elevations are drawn from the 26 August site visit and Concurrent's published cabinet dimensions; the door aperture height is still unconfirmed and is drawn as an estimate. No hardware has been bought and nothing has been fitted to the machine.
